analysis.one_liner: Taxes tobacco companies tens of billions a year, puts nicotine under FDA regulation, and funds anti-smoking programs to cut youth tobacco use.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: introduced March 31, 1998 with two cosponsors, it was read twice, placed on the Senate calendar, and sat there until the Congress ended January 3, 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The KIDS Act would have made tobacco companies pay $10 billion up front and up to $25 billion a year into a public health fund, handed the Food and Drug Administration authority to regulate tobacco products, imposed stiff penalties if youth smoking didn't fall by set percentages, restricted advertising and youth access, and paid states back for treating tobacco-related illness. Tobacco companies would have to raise cigarette prices by at least $1.00 to $1.50 a pack to cover the payments. The bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face higher cigarette prices, restricted advertising, licensed and tracked retail sales, and penalties on manufacturers if underage smoking failed to fall as much as 65 percent by 2008. Smokers who want to quit would get federally funded cessation programs. States would be reimbursed for treating tobacco-related illness, with at least half the money required to go to programs like Medicaid, children's health insurance, Head Start, and child care. Sicker smokers and their families would be compensated through a victims' fund, and the public would get access to tobacco companies' internal documents on addiction and health effects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, smokers trying to quit, and states

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must pay $10 billion within 90 days, $20 billion the next year, and $25 billion annually thereafter, adjusted for inflation, into a National Tobacco Trust Fund [S2, S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services must impose escalating industry-wide and company-specific penalties if underage tobacco use does not fall at least 15 percent by 2000 and 65 percent by 2008, and those penalties are not tax deductible [S2, S3].

The bill confirms FDA authority over tobacco as a drug and device, mandates warning labels, ingredient disclosure, release of industry research on addiction and health effects, and a public document depository [S2, S3].

At least half of each state's payment must go to health and children's programs, including Medicaid, children's health insurance, community health centers, Head Start, child care, and public education [S2, S3].
Manufacturers are required to raise prices by at least $1.00 per pack for the second payment and another $0.50 for annual payments, a price increase designed to reduce smoking [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers, who bear the assessments, penalties, licensing fees, FDA regulation, and forced price increases — and, because the bill requires companies to pass the costs through, smokers would pay roughly $1.50 more per pack. Small retailers would face federal registration fees per store and limits like a 50-package-per-transaction cap. Tobacco farm families would have had to rely on a separate assistance fund that only activated if Congress passed follow-up legislation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tobacco companies and, through price mandates, smokers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires manufacturers to pass the assessments to consumers through price increases of at least $1.00 to $1.50 per pack, so much of the cost falls on adult smokers, including low-income ones, rather than on company shareholders [S3].

In exchange for state payments, the bill requires states to settle pending lawsuits against tobacco companies and bars them from filing new ones to recover treatment costs, terminating class addiction claims — a trade of litigation rights for a statutory settlement [S2].

Manufacturers that had already settled with more than 25 states before January 1, 1998 are exempted from the initial payment and 40 percent of annual assessments, tilting the cost toward companies that had not settled [S3].
Total penalties for missing youth-reduction targets are capped at $10 billion per year, a limit an honest supporter would acknowledge softens the enforcement pressure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a comprehensive attempt to price, regulate, and penalize tobacco companies to cut youth smoking, with real money flowing to children's health programs and state reimbursements. Its honest costs are that smokers, not shareholders, pay most of the assessment through a mandated price increase, and that it trades away state lawsuits and some private claims in exchange for the payments. The industry also kept carve-outs for early settlers and a capped penalty schedule. On balance it imposed real costs on a concentrated industry while delivering broad public health benefits, but its design mixed consumer-funded payments with industry penalties.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and placed on the Senate calendar, but it never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin introduced the KIDS Act on March 31, 1998, joined by Sens. Chafee and Graham [S3, S1].
The bill was read a first time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar, then read a second time on April 1, 1998 and placed on the calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 333 [S5, S3].
That was the last action: the record shows no committee referral, hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they never paid the assessments, faced no FDA authority from this bill, and the private-document disclosure never happened. Adult smokers also avoided the mandated price increase, but the bill's targets — preventing youth smoking — went unmet by this measure.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the KIDS Act and delivered introductory remarks on March 31, 1998 [S5, S3].

for.name: Sen. John Chafee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Rhode Island, cosponsor

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: In 1998 the industry mounted a large-scale advertising and lobbying campaign against comprehensive tobacco legislation, framing it as a big-government tax; the Senate's main tobacco bill failed on a procedural vote in June 1998, and no tobacco settlement bill advanced after that.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee or floor consideration; it sat on the Senate calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The record is too thin to show a party split: the bill had only two cosponsors, one Republican (Chafee) and one Democrat (Graham), and never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed $10 billion in immediate payments and $25 billion a year thereafter, FDA regulation, licensing, mandatory document disclosure, and youth-reduction penalties on manufacturers. It also would have resolved state lawsuits against them, but only in exchange for the payments, disclosure, and consent-decree obligations.

Retailers would have faced federal registration and fees per store and transaction limits, costs that fall on small businesses. The same licensing system was designed to stop underage sales and contraband trafficking.

industries.industry: Tobacco farm families and tobacco-growing communities
industries.note: The bill created a trust fund to assist tobacco-dependent farm families, workers, and communities, though it would only have taken effect if Congress passed follow-up legislation specifying the uses.

industries.industry: Health insurers, public health programs, and research institutions
industries.note: State reimbursements had to flow at least half into Medicaid, children's health insurance, community health centers, and children's programs, and a share of the fund went to NIH institutes, CDC research, and smoking-cessation services.
